pedagogy.summary: Rounding a one-decimal-place number to the nearest whole means deciding which of the two neighbouring whole numbers it is closest to on the number line — the tenths digit tells you which half you are in. The 'round up at 5' rule is a CONVENTION for the exact midpoint (x.5), which is genuinely equidistant. It is best taught as 'nearest' on a number line, from which the digit rule is derived, not as a first-move recipe for chopping or bumping digits.
bestPractices: Put the decimal on a number line between its two whole neighbours and ask 'which is it nearer?' before any rule
Mark the halfway point (e.g. 3.5) and treat 'round up at the midpoint' as an agreed convention introduced only once 'nearest' is secure
Distinguish rounding from truncating: 3.7 rounds to 4, it is not chopped to 3
Round to the NEAREST — resist teaching 'if there's anything after the point, go up' (that sends 3.2 to 4)
Have children round a set and articulate the rule as a consequence of distance, then check by estimating
keyRepresentations: Number line 3–4 with 3.7 plotted and 3.5 marked as halfway
Bead string / hundred square segment between two wholes
A 'rounding hill' where a ball rolls to the nearer whole
commonMisconceptions: Truncates — drops the decimal and always rounds down (3.7 → 3)
Always rounds up when any decimal part is present (3.2 → 4)
Thinks the exact midpoint 3.5 rounds down, or is unsure what to do with it
Confuses rounding with changing the digit (3.7 → 3.10 / 4.0 muddle)

learn.summary: Rounding a one-decimal-place number to the nearest whole number means deciding which of the two neighbouring whole numbers it lies closest to on a number line — the tenths digit tells you which half of the interval you are in. The 'round up at 5' rule is a CONVENTION for the exact midpoint (x.5), which is genuinely equidistant from both wholes. It is best taught as 'nearest' on a number line, from which the digit rule is then derived, rather than as a first-move recipe for chopping or bumping digits. Target age 8–9 (Year 4).

activities.title: Which whole is it nearest? Placing decimals on a number line
feedback: If a learner gives 3 for 3.7: on the number line show that 3.7 is only 0.3 away from 4 but 0.7 away from 3, so it is nearer 4; contrast this with simply chopping off the part after the point.
If a learner gives 4 for 3.2: mark the halfway point 3.5 and show 3.2 sits below it, in the lower half, so it is nearer 3 — having 'something after the point' does not automatically mean round up.
If a learner is unsure what rounding means: contrast rounding 3.7 (to 4, the nearer whole) with chopping/truncating 3.7 (to 3, just dropping the part after the point) so the difference is explicit.
Reinforce correct reasoning by asking the learner to justify each answer by distance rather than by reciting a rule.
activities.rationale: Positioning the decimal between its two whole neighbours and asking 'which is it nearer?' is intended to make 'nearest' the felt basis of the rule and to help address the two dominant errors (truncating always-down and always-up). Statutory curriculum expects Year 4 pupils to round decimals with 1 decimal place to the nearest whole number, and guidance recommends understanding rounding as choosing between the two candidate values a number lies between.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils are taught to 'round decimals with 1 decimal place to the nearest whole number' (verbatim statutory wording, Year 4 Number - fractions including decimals).

Rounding should be understood as choosing between the two candidate values a number lies between - 'one just greater and one just less' - with a number line used to see which the number is closer to; 'memorising and applying a procedure for rounding... without this overall awareness often results in errors', producing errors such as cascading 'keep rounding up' (3472 to 4000) and assuming a decimal less than one like 0.512 rounds to 1 because 0.5 does.
learnerActions: Draw or use a number line from 3 to 4 with each tenth marked, and plot 3.7 on it.
Ask aloud: is 3.7 nearer to 3 or to 4, and roughly how much nearer? Measure or count the gaps (0.3 to 4, 0.7 to 3).
Plot 3.2 on the same line and decide which whole it is nearer, explaining from the position (0.2 to 3, 0.8 to 4).
Mark the halfway point 3.5 and say what is special about it.
Repeat with a fresh set of one-decimal-place numbers (e.g. 2.8, 5.1, 7.4), stating each result and why.

Finally state the rule in your own words as a consequence of distance: 'look at the tenths — if it is in the lower half it rounds down, in the upper half it rounds up, and the exact midpoint follows the agreed convention.'
activities.intendedInsight: Rounding is a nearness judgement on a line: the whole you round to is the one the number is closer to. The tenths digit is a shortcut that reports which half of the interval you are in, not an arbitrary 'chop or bump' instruction.

activities.title: The midpoint x.5 and the round-up convention
feedback: If a learner gives 6 for 6.5 or hesitates: establish first that 6.5 is equidistant from 6 and 7, then introduce 'round half up' as a shared rule everyone agrees to use.
If a learner thinks the midpoint 'obviously' goes up for a distance reason: clarify that both wholes are exactly as far away, so the up-choice is a convention, not because 7 is nearer.
Praise a learner who can say 6.5 is the special equidistant case and that the convention is a choice.
activities.rationale: Separating the equidistant midpoint from ordinary nearness cases is intended to help address the misconception that the midpoint defaults down or is undefined, and correctly frames 'round half up' as a convention. This builds on, rather than replaces, the number-line understanding of 'nearest'.
sourceClaims: Rounding should be understood as choosing between the two candidate values a number lies between - 'one just greater and one just less' - with a number line used to see which the number is closer to; 'memorising and applying a procedure for rounding... without this overall awareness often results in errors', producing errors such as cascading 'keep rounding up' (3472 to 4000) and assuming a decimal less than one like 0.512 rounds to 1 because 0.5 does.
learnerActions: On a number line from 6 to 7, place 6.5 and measure its distance to 6 and to 7.
Confirm that 6.5 is exactly halfway — equally far from both wholes — so distance alone cannot decide.
Discuss who decides what happens here, and learn that the agreed convention is 'round half up', so 6.5 rounds to 7.
Try other midpoints (e.g. 2.5, 4.5) and apply the same agreed convention, stating that this is a shared choice, not a distance fact.
Explain in your own words the difference between 6.5 (needs the convention) and 6.7 (decided by nearness).
activities.intendedInsight: The exact midpoint is the one case nearness does not settle because it is equidistant; 'round half up' is an agreed convention introduced once 'nearest' is secure, not an extension of the distance rule.

activities.title: Sort and check a set of roundings
feedback: If a learner sorts 3.5 into 'rounds to 3': remind them it is the equidistant midpoint and the agreed convention sends it up to 4.
If a learner sorts 3.2 into 'rounds to 4': return to the halfway mark and show 3.2 is in the lower half, nearer 3.
If a learner sorts everything with a decimal into 'rounds to 4': this is the always-up error — check each against the midpoint.
Confirm a correct sort by asking the learner to re-state the rule as a consequence of nearness.
activities.rationale: Practising over a varied set surfaces both truncation and always-up errors across many cases, and requiring a distance justification keeps the rule grounded in 'nearest' rather than a memorised recipe. This is a consolidation/checking activity rather than the initial teaching.
learnerActions: Take a mixed set of one-decimal-place numbers (e.g. 3.1, 3.7, 3.5, 3.4, 3.8, 3.2) and sort each into 'rounds to 3' or 'rounds to 4'.
For each number, say its distance to each whole, or which half it is in, to justify your sort.

Round 3.7 correctly to 4, then show the two common error patterns on the numbers where each actually goes wrong: truncation wrongly gives 3 for 3.7 (dropping the part after the point), while the always-up error wrongly sends numbers like 3.2 to 4.
Check your whole set by estimating and asking whether each answer is sensible.
State the rounding rule aloud as a summary of what the sort shows.
activities.intendedInsight: Rounding a set is cleanly checkable, and articulating why each number rounds as it does consolidates the distance-based reason behind the digit rule.

constraints: Teach 'nearest' on a number line FIRST; introduce the 'round up at 5' rule only afterwards and only for the exact midpoint, framed as an agreed convention, not a distance fact.
Do not teach 'if there is anything after the point, go up' — that wrongly sends 3.2 to 4. The tenths digit indicates which half of the interval the number is in.
Distinguish rounding from truncating explicitly: 3.7 rounds to 4; it is not chopped to 3.
Avoid muddling rounding with changing digits (e.g. 3.7 becoming 3.10 or a stray 4.0 confusion); the result is a whole number.

When illustrating error patterns, attach each error to a number where it actually produces a wrong answer: truncation errs on 3.7 (gives 3), always-up errs on 3.2 (gives 4). Do not present the always-up answer (4) as a 'wrong move' for 3.7, whose correct answer is 4.

A static labelled number line with tap-to-reveal can display one rounding as a reference aid, but it does not let a learner test many cases or feel why the midpoint is special, so it is a scaffold rather than the main teaching tool.
Selecting a rounded answer from options checks the outcome but does not by itself elicit the distance justification; pair any selection task with a spoken or written 'why'.
A number line captures nearness in one dimension; added depth or 3D representation is not needed here, though it is not claimed to be harmful.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and no comparative efficacy of any particular activity format is claimed.

Self-audit of the arithmetic and logic: 3.7 is 0.3 from 4 and 0.7 from 3, so it is nearer 4 (rounds to 4) — correct. 3.2 is 0.2 from 3 and 0.8 from 4, nearer 3 (rounds to 3) — correct. 6.5 and 3.5 are exactly equidistant, so 'round half up' is correctly presented as a convention, not a distance consequence. The sort set {3.1, 3.7, 3.5, 3.4, 3.8, 3.2} resolves to rounds-to-3 {3.1, 3.4, 3.2} and rounds-to-4 {3.7, 3.8, 3.5} — consistent.
Confirmed the third activity does not treat 4 as a wrong answer for 3.7: 3.7 rounds correctly to 4, and the always-up error is attached to numbers like 3.2.
The source's diagnostic distinctions (truncation 3,3,6; always-up 4,4,7; secure 4,3,7) are internally consistent and preserved across the feedback branches.

Softened one rationale from 'directly confronts' to 'is intended to help address' so no untested activity format carries an unqualified efficacy claim; both cited sources support the number-line 'nearest' framing only, not any specific implementation.

probeDeeper: On the number line, is 3.7 nearer to 3 or to 4 — and roughly how much nearer?
Which whole is 3.2 closer to? How can you tell from the tenths digit?
6.5 is exactly halfway between 6 and 7 — so which one do we round to, and who decides that?
Does 'round' mean chop off the part after the point? What is different about rounding 3.7 and chopping 3.7?
assess.correctAnswer: 3.7 → 4 (nearer 4), 3.2 → 3 (nearer 3), 6.5 → 7 (exact midpoint, rounds up by convention). Justifies each by distance on the number line.

errorPatterns.pattern: Truncates — chops the decimal and rounds everything down: 3.7 → 3
errorPatterns.nextMove: On the number line, ask which whole 3.7 is nearer and by how much; contrast rounding with chopping explicitly.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives 3 for 3.7; ignores the tenths digit entirely; treats 'round' as 'drop the bit after the point'

errorPatterns.pattern: Rounds up whenever any decimal part is present: 3.2 → 4 ('there's a bit after the point so go up')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Mark the halfway point; show 3.2 sits below it, in the lower half, so it is nearer 3.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives 4 for 3.2; rounds up regardless of the size of the tenths

errorPatterns.pattern: Rounds the midpoint the wrong way or is unsure — 6.5 → 6, treating 'nearest' as undefined and defaulting down
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish that 6.5 is exactly halfway (equal distance to 6 and 7), then introduce the agreed 'round half up' convention as a shared rule.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives 6 for 6.5, or hesitates and guesses; does not recognise it as equidistant

responseLevels.gap: Truncates (always down) or always rounds up regardless of the tenths; shows no sense of 'nearest'.
responseLevels.full: Rounds all three correctly, explains 3.7 is nearer 4 and 3.2 nearer 3, treats 6.5 as the midpoint that rounds up by convention, states the rule as a consequence of nearest, and transfers to a fresh set.
responseLevels.partial: Rounds 3.7 and 3.2 correctly by nearness on the line, but is unsure at the 6.5 midpoint, or applies '5 and up' without seeing it comes from distance.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'Round 3.7 to the nearest whole number, then 3.2, then 6.5. For each one, show me on a number line why you chose that whole.' Watch how they decide — do not give a rule.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The three cases pull apart the common errors: a truncator says 3, 3, 6; an always-up child says 4, 4, 7; a secure child says 4, 3, 7 and can explain WHY 6.5 is the special midpoint case. 6.5 is the hinge — only a child who understands 'nearest' recognises it as equidistant and knows the round-up convention is a choice, not a distance fact.
